speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
We have reached orders of the day, and the rules of the house do not determine what the precedence is for the day. I am in the position of not being able to call an order without the direction of the house or resolving the problem which is now raised, since it is my duty to call an order of the day.
If I might indicate the situation, which I think hon. members probably appreciate, may I point out that standing order 15 settles the business of the house. Subsection 2 of standing order 15 settles the daily routine for every day, and we have passed through that procedure. Then it gives the orders of the day. They are settled from Monday to Friday by standing order 15, but no provision is made for Saturday. By order made on Monday, April 24, the house has decided to sit today and every Saturday until the end of the session without specifying the order of business. I refer to Votes and Proceedings

for Monday, April 24, page 467, where an order was made for the house to sit on Saturday from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m.
On the order paper, without precedence being assigned to them, are the orders the house has appointed for consideration today and every day, namely government orders, public bills and orders, notices of motions for production of papers, private bills and starred questions. They are printed on the order paper and, as I say, have all been ordered by the house for consideration today or any day the house meets.
The problem that arises, of course, is what the precedence is among these orders. As the order paper indicates, I have not taken the responsibility of determining what precedence should be given to the orders, but have simply caused them to be printed in the order in which they appeared on Friday, the last sitting day.
I raise this matter as a point of order for disposition with the assistance of the house, and I suggest two approaches to the problem. First, as the house has ordered no business for today, and as it has ordered certain hours of sitting, I think the presumption is that the house intends to do some business. I think the question as to the precedence of the business should be resolved in a way which is permissible under the rules. In other words, I think the solution should be one in favour of carrying out the orders of the house in so far as they have been made.
The problem is that the order did not go quite far enough. There are two approaches to this question, and I suggest them for the consideration of the house. One is this. In the absence of any rule, our standing order No. 1 refers us to the procedure of the parliament of the United Kingdom, and hon. members may find some indication by that means. I have made some inquiry on my own initiative, and I refer the house to Campion's "Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons", page 132, which does not go very far but is as follows:
On Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday the house meets at half past two and adjourns normally at half past ten, or later. (S.O. No. 1). On Friday the corresponding hours are eleven a.m. and half past four p.m. (S.O.s No. 1 and 2). These hours were last fixed by amendments to standing orders made in 1947.
The house seldom sits on Saturday and only in case of grave emergency on Sunday. Unless otherwise fixed, the hour for meeting on Saturday follows the rule for Friday. There is no prescribed hour for a Sunday sitting.
That does not deal with the business to be done other than by inference.
90205-6-281J
Business of the House
The other approach is that the house is the master of its own proceedings. In circumstances where direction is necessary, it has the power to deal with procedural problems that arise.
Having said that, I am not disposed to make any decision but to ask for consideration of the point of order which arises. Perhaps I should hear the pro and the con in the usual order, and I will first hear the house leader.

but I submit it is master of its own proceedings within and in accordance with the rules of the house only. The house leader has said that the house decided on an earlier occasion that it would sit this day for the purpose of conducting business. I challenge that statement. The house made no such decision. If the motion made last night by the house leader had passed, of course the orders of the day would have contained what we now find on page 4. The printing could not have been other than it is now. It has been stated that the business should be as it now appears at page 4. I cannot agree with that statement, because page 4 does not come into effect until the required rules of the house have been complied with.
Finally, the house leader has said this matter is within the competence of the Speaker. I say to you respectfully, and I am sure you, sir, are of the same view, that the Speaker, while he interprets the rules of the house, is also himself bound by and subject to the rules of the house. He is the one who applies the rules, and in applying the rules he must make sure that in a motion such as this, 48 hours' notice is given. It cannot be given with reference to the motion which is now before Your Honour; therefore the rules have not been complied with. I may be permitted to speak for a few minutes on the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like our position to be very clearly understood. We feel very strongly, sir, that in order to ensure the efficient operation of the House of Commons there must be the strictest possible adherence to the standing orders and customs of the house. It has already been made clear, sir, that our standing orders and customs in this Canadian House of Commons give us no indication as to how to proceed. As you, sir, have rightly pointed out in your quotation, if the United Kingdom parliament sits on a Saturday without any prior order of precedence under standing orders, then automatically the business on Saturday follows the precedence of business on Friday. We submit, therefore, that since under our standing orders there is no order, precedent or custom for a motion such as the house leader has sought to move

Business of the House

Second, there being no standing order, custom or precedent for this situation, then according to our standing orders it is your duty to proceed with the business of the house on this Saturday in accordance with the customs and precedents of the United Kingdom parliament, which means we would follow the order of business for Friday.
If these courses are not followed, sir, then we most respectfully submit there is only one motion that can be accepted in this house, namely that we stand adjourned until 11 o'clock on Monday morning. Therefore it is my duty to interpret the rules in a way which does not lead to a denial of those two orders. To my mind it would be an absurdity to convene and then, because of some error, do no business.
It is not my business to commend or otherwise; I simply am obliged to deal with the situation with which we are faced. Because of a deficiency, shall we say, in the order of the business of the house, a problem arises which calls for a solution that at least makes sense. It seems to me that any solution which left the house suspended, with no business at all to do, would not make sense.
It has been proposed to meet the difficulty by a motion, and I have been concerned to ascertain whether that motion could be entertained. It is not a motion under standing
Business of the House
order 41 which requires 48 hours' notice, in my judgment, because it is a motion to order the business of the house. It is not a bill or a resolution that requires 48 hours' notice. It is a motion with respect to the business of the house; it is a motion to make an order of the house, which order can be made without notice. Furthermore, we have not yet entered upon orders of the day, for the good reason that I was not prepared to call an order of the day until I had the advice of the house. We are therefore on routine proceedings, and there are motions relating to the business of the house that can be made on routine proceedings.
The point has been taken that the motion should have been made when motions were being dealt with-and I think it should have been made at that time-rather than after we had passed from motions to government notices of motions. However, if the matter were pressed or considered further I think some ground might be found for entertaining the motion. I therefore do not discard the possibility of a motion without notice on routine proceedings. speechtext:
If I may answer the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I adjourned this debate; therefore I was prepared to start in, no matter when it came up.
I was amazed this morning at the suggestion from the Liberal members that the bill before us was controversial. I would have thought that because of its importance to agriculture it would have received the unanimous support of all hon. members. As a western member and representing one of the best farming areas in all Canada, I am happy to have the opportunity to support Bill No. C-77, to provide for the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada.
Other members have spoken on this measure and have outlined its general principles. I need not repeat those statements, but I do wish to reiterate their remarks about our very able and energetic Minister of Agriculture and add to the congratulations extended to him for the good work he is doing on behalf of agriculture and Canadian farmers. The
Marginal Lands Development recent announcement by the minister of the three year agreement with China for the sale of grain to the value of $425,600,000 emphasizes that these congratulations are merited. As he stated, these sales of grain will be of great benefit to the Canadian economy through increased farm income and higher employment.
All Canada welcomes this announcement. I should like to draw these remarks to the attention of the hon. member for Assiniboia. I was amazed at his attack in the house on this agreement. I asked him at that time if he was speaking for the New party or personally and he did not answer me. Perhaps he will answer later.
In extending congratulations to the Minister of Agriculture I do not want to minimize in any way the fine work of his predecessor in initiating long range government farm policies that are now beginning to have a very noticeable effect. In Bill No. C-77 the present minister is continuing these long range measures of the government.
One of the valuable contributions the minister is making toward greater understanding of the government's farm policy is the heavy program of personal visits to all parts of Canada that he has undertaken. He has had great success in explaining what the government is attempting to do, and is doing for the farmers. I know the farmers in my area appreciate the minister's very clear outline of the policies of his department. One of his first public addresses after assuming his new portfolio was in Moose Jaw, where he spoke to 200 or more practical farmers and a large number of businessmen. The theme of his address was along the lines of what is contained in Bill No. C-77, the need for the active interest and co-operation of businessmen and all non-farm groups to help to bolster farm income for the benefit of all segments of the economy.
As I said, his Moose Jaw address was one of the minister's first speeches outlining his ideas as to what must be done for agriculture. It was one of his first direct references to the legislation respecting agricultural rehabilitation and development envisaged by the bill before us. When the bill is passed it will embody the minister's great hope of having the federal government, the provincial governments and all interested groups and individuals work together to improve the income position of Canadian farmers, for the benefit of all.
I have had considerable correspondence with farmers in my constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre since the minister's address in Moose Jaw. These letters show that the farmers in my area, a predominantly wheat growing district, are thinking very seriously about their situation. I believe they see what

Marginal Lands Development the federal government is doing for them, and understand what is involved in Bill No. C-77. I received a letter recently from a prominent farmer in my constituency, and I took the liberty of sending his comments to the minister. I think they will encourage the minister to continue along the lines the government is now following.
The writer of the letter is Mr. Wilfred McKenzie of Belbeck, Saskatchewan, which is north of Moose Jaw. Mr. McKenzie has always taken a very active interest in farm programs. He succeeded me as chairman of the agricultural committee of the Moose Jaw chamber of commerce, and in this position is a direct link between the farmers and the city businessmen. In his letter Mr. McKenzie made these comments, among others:
It would appear that the problems of agriculture are not getting any less, but I am wondering if the time is not fast approaching when almost everything else but agriculture will be the problem. It could be that agriculture has probably stayed the closest to the right perspective and most everything else has been on the rampage and will find it the more difficult to level out. I would think that so far as the world economy is concerned agriculture has been more in line, with the result the adjustment may eventually fall the hardest on industry.
If agriculture would hold the line and not try to go forward at this time, it might not be too long before it will be the front line and also the line that Canada will badly need to fall back on, especially for the labour force. It might be a good idea if we all took a long look backward and then look forward with a realistic view dominating our idealistic view.
I think these views support the principle of Bill No. C-77. They are the views of a very practical farmer. I am glad to have the opportunity to bring them to the attention of the minister and the members of the house. I was impressed by Mr. McKenzie's proposal that we look forward. This forward look is exactly what the A.R.D.A., when passed, will undertake.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
I have indicated the name of the author. I would be pleased to table the letter. I should like to conclude my reference to this newspaper report. The speaker warned that prairie soils are showing evidence of depleted soil fertility. Here is one of his direct statements:
Improper use of our land has ruined or seriously damaged an estimated 13 million acres.
This bill, No. C-77, Mr. Speaker, is an answer to this serious problem. It is interesting to note that it was a Conservative government that took the first step along the lines of the provisions contained in this bill. This fact is indicated in an article in the Lumsden weekly from my constituency under the heading "How federal rehabilitation efforts have

aided agriculture in the past and will provide further assistance in the future". I quote from that article:
Thirty years ago a worried federal government undertook a rather drastic course of action to assist agriculture in western Canada to fight its way out of a depression that was aggravated by drought, erosion, insects and disease.
Today, another government stands on the threshold of yet another program of assistance to agriculture-and there are similarities.
The first program introduced through the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, took direct action toward rehabilitating thousands of desolated acres in the west. It also worked indirectly, teaching by example at many experimental farms and substations.
The article states, at another point:
Vigorous rehabilitation measures changed the picture.
The article then concludes as follows:
In the same way, the new redevelopment program about to be launched will undoubtedly move agriculture up several more rungs in the ladder of success.
I think I should add to the article this statement made by the Minister of Agriculture when he moved the resolution preceding this measure on January 25. Here is what he said at that time as reported on page 1403 of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, in moving the adoption of this resolution I do so with the full realization that it will constitute a major step forward in fulfilling our national agricultural program presented to the house on August 30, 1958, by the Prime Minister.
I want to commend the minister and his department for the production of this little pamphlet "ARDA". I should like to draw the attention of the house to the outline on the back page which refers to the percentage of farms, by provinces, having an annual potential production of less than $1,200. For Canada as a whole, this outline shows 21 per cent of the farmers have an annual income of less than $1,200. Saskatchewan has the best record with only 4 per cent of its farmers with annual incomes of less than $1,200.
I should also like to put on record a statement by the minister under the heading "Reduction of Farms Not Purpose of A.R.D.A." Here is his statement:
It is not the purpose of A.R.D.A. to reduce the number of farms . . . A.R.D.A. Is designed, rather, to help by various means to improve the income and standard of living of the smaller and more marginal farms, and in that way help improve the over-all position of agriculture.
In an address to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture the minister suggested that everyone associated with the farming business should dedicate the next few years to an objective assessment of where we stand and where we are going. That is what the federal government is attempting to do by this legislation.
Marginal Lands Development
I have here a clipping from the Western Producer of January 26, 1961, reporting a statement by Dr. H. H. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Dr. Hannam says that the federation for years has been urging the type of program envisaged in this bill. He added that farmers will be faced with a major challenge to their imagination when the act comes into effect, because it will open up broad opportunities for action in the fields of soil and water conservation, land use development and rural economic development in general. He concluded that farmers will have a responsibility along with governments to see that the legislation is used effectively and extensively.
In this regard there are some interesting statements in volume No. 8 of the proceedings of the special committee of the other place on land use in Canada, April 26 and April 27. As found at page 204, Mr. Ross Hill, executive director of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture states:
I wish to point out that whatever a farmer produces comes from the land in some form, and therefore all the social and economic changes through the years have been dependent on the manner in which our land resources have been managed. There is every reason to believe that even greater emphasis will be placed on land use and land values in the future, because of the evolution which has taken place in our industry.
As found at page 209 Dr. C. C. Spence, economics division, Canadian Department of Agriculture, Edmonton, Alberta, under the heading of "Irrigation in Canada and its Impact on Agriculture" states:
From the irrigation experience in Canada as related it is obvious that any estimates as to the acreage which should be developed in irrigation and its location in the future could be very far off without careful and co-ordinating studies of water supply, engineering, efficiency in use of water, land, climate, markets and even human attitudes.
These statements repeat what has already been said about the realistic forward look for agriculture that the minister proposes to undertake under the terms of this bill. I wish to emphasize the need for co-operation from the provincial governments in this rehabilitation program; and because I come from Saskatchewan I make this appeal for co-operation directly to the Saskatchewan government. As the minister has pointed out, one of the key points in this legislation will be the widest possible participation not only by farmers but by every group in our rural communities. Agricultural rehabilitation and development calls for the combined enterprise of governments, groups and individuals. This bill will help farmers help themselves. It will also bring other segments of our economy into the battle for a more stabilized

Marginal Lands Development agricultural industry. The farmers need and will welcome this co-ordinated help.
If I may conclude with another brief reference to the China wheat deal which is part and parcel of the better days for agriculture envisaged by the bill, I wish to assure the Minister of Agriculture that I have already received from constituents letters commending him on his efforts to sell more wheat than has been sold in many years, with the prospects of still greater sales. Again may I say that I am happy to support this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time in order to add a few words to the discussion which has already been lengthy on this A.R.D.A. bill.
I do so at this time because I have 6,000 farmers in my riding. I have heard words of commendation from every source, from groups and from individual farmers, by correspondence, as to the high regard they have for this bill which we hope will soon be enacted.
I now wish to take up one or two points which this bill seeks to accomplish. The first objective is to get at marginal and low productivity land. What is envisaged is to have an instrument of human making to get at, in an economic and physical way, the adjustments to which marginal and low productivity land are subject and which often take so many years to work out. During that long waiting period when these adjustments are working out, the farmers are run through the wringer because of low income and because of the lack of any policy to assist them t.o make an adjustment.
This bill seeks to provide the farmers with an act which will assist them in making these adjustments. In other words, as was stated by the hon. member who has just spoken, it will assist the farmer to help himself. I wish to say that, judging from previous experience, we shall have some difficulties in administering this act. There will be many discussions among the farmers on the question of marginal lands, for example. Let us take a moment in order to discuss that matter. What do we mean by marginal land? For what reason is it marginal? It may be marginal because it is of low productivity, or because of the frost free period of the locality in which the land is situated. It may be marginal because of the lack of rainfall or because of the location of the land. You might also add that it may be marginal because of the type of managerial policy of the person who is operating it. You can now add up the items in that list. All of them add up to what we mean in economic terms as the causes of marginal land.
If a piece of land is marginal in its present use, the thought behind this legislation
[Mr. Pascoe.l
is to see what can be done to improve its productivity and use, and at the same time take care of the farmers who are at present engaged in farming such land.
What is needed is the development of income and employment opportunities for rural and agricultural people. In many areas the size of the business unit is too small. Where possible we should combine some of these units and change the type of use to a more extensive one, or it may go the other way, to a more intensified type of use. In this way by planning and by a program of action we could bring about a higher income for farmers and a more profitable use of the land.
In addition to that it should be pointed out that you cannot isolate any one problem in an area, treat it by itself and completely neglect all the other. You have to think about new industries, supplementary industries and the development of other means of earning an income, or at least a supplementary income, for those farmers who are operating on small units.
At Fort MacLeod we have just completed one of the finest pieces of industrial development that I think has come about in southwestern Alberta in the past decade or more. The old airport there was sold to the town of Fort MacLeod and they have set about to develop industry and move industries into each of the hangars. At the present time a new industry has moved in from Estevan, Saskatchewan, and is employing approximately 65 people. Another is moving in to start up a plywood plant which will employ 50 people. This industry will be shipping raw materials in from the Crowsnest pass and eastern British Columbia. There are two other industries which I do not care to mention, which are seriously considering moving in.
The present situation is that this town has within the last three months increased its population by at least 500 people, and it may even increase it by 1,000 people. This has been done by developing supplementary industries which might have gone by the board had the authorities not moved in the right direction.
It is this type of planning which must be done by local communities. This type of planning has already been done by the people of Fort MacLeod, who have demonstrated that it can be done.
We are now in the midst of undertaking a similar transfer of the Claresholm airport to the town of Claresholm or perhaps to the municipal district of Willow Creek if arrangements can be made. In other words, in all these communities we are hoping to obtain

local development and at the same time assist marginal farmers and low income farmers to supplement their incomes.
There is one other point I should like to mention in connection with this broad, general program introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton). I refer to the conservation of soil and water. One has only to study the history of China to see that down through the ages the loss of soil there has almost ruined certain sections of the country. We also find in that study that these people have made efforts over past hundreds of years to maintain the fertility of their soil. They have put organic matter back into the soil; they have never lost an opportunity to add fertility or to till the soil in such a manner as to maintain its fertility. However, in spite of their efforts they have suffered a tremendous amount of soil erosion and in many, many cases the loss of a high percentage of the topsoil.
One has only to go to the prairie provinces to see this illustrated. One has only to look at the farmers who are farming land up and down these hills, and then take another look at these areas following a heavy rainfall. You find that the hillsides have been gullied and tremendous quantities of topsoil have been washed off, never to be returned. It is plowing on the contour, farming these lands on the contour, the seeding of grasses, rotation of crops, restoration of fibre and the fertility of the soil which are problems with which the practical farmer must grapple. These are the problems to which this particular program must give attention and assist the farmer to overcome.
In other words, it often happens that the financial resources of an individual farmer are insufficient for him to do the things he would like to do. It is therefore hoped that this program will come in time and give every possible assistance to help bring about adjustments in the farming pattern of the land. This program will cost in the neighbourhood of $300 million to $600 million spread over the next decade. I wish to say that it is the best way in which this or any other government could spend money in helping to bring about these land use adjustments in agriculture; that is, to maintain the fertility of the soil and the economic use of the water that falls as related to the production of food, which of course is of tremendous interest to us all.
If a country loses the fertility of its soils- and one has only to study what has happened in the past ages where the fertility of soil has been lost-you will find the people in the affected areas perish. This has been the pattern in the past.
Marginal Lands Development
Therefore we in Canada must take a hard look at what we are doing with our soils. I have only to refer to the experience of farmers in my area, and in fact to my experience on our own farm, which has been farmed for some 40 or 50 years, to illustrate my point. The fertility of the soil is going down; hilltops become more exposed, rocks are showing and the productivity of the land at those spots is becoming depleted.
In other words, unless we change our methods and assist farmers to change their methods in order to bring about a better use of soil and a better use of our resources, the day will come when we will have no topsoil and everybody in society will suffer. Therefore this legislation strikes right at the very heart of everybody's vested interests in that it deals with maintaining the fertility of the soil.
Changes will be needed in this legislation as time goes by. It will need amendments and it will go through a process of evolution based on experience. But there is nothing wrong with that; that is the very thing that should happen.
I should like to refer to an article appearing in the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, May 4, 1961 under the heading "Mr. Pearson hides his light under 275,800,000 bushels". This was an editorial which appeared in that edition of the paper regarding the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture in the house concerning the sale of wheat to China. I should like to say that I was present at the time and I consider the minister's statement to be one of the most profound I have heard in many years. Speaking on behalf of the farmers, particularly in my area, I may say they are exuberant over this announcement.
I was very much disturbed by the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and I should have thought he in turn would have lent his wholehearted support to this move and refrained from casting doubt for political purposes.
When one travels around the country one is impressed with the fact that this wheat agreement is of tremendous significance and usefulness to Canada's wheat trade and to the present economic situation generally. Whether one views this move in terms of agriculture, prairie farm conditions, railway freight or port activity, unemployment, or even a general boom in business, this projected sale will be of tremendous benefit to Canada's economy as a whole. I want to compliment the Minister of Agriculture in this regard on behalf of the 6,000 farmers in my riding who are so well pleased with what has been accomplished.
In conclusion, I should like to suggest that the bill now before us should receive the

Marginal Lands Development heartiest endorsation by this house because the people want this A.R.D.A. legislation and it is needed for the future national development of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had of speaking on a Saturday afternoon in this session, and I must say that I find it delightful. I rise at this time to make a few remarks in explanation of several matters involved in our program of rehabilitation of agricultural land as it affects the area in my constituency.
The members of my party feel very pleased with this bill, as I am sure the minister does. The majority of hon. members in the opposition seem to feel the proposed bill is good, although they have perhaps not directly said so. We feel this is the logical continuation of agricultural programs such as the Agricultural Stabilization Act and the Farm Credit Act as well as perhaps the Crop Insurance Act.
As one hon. member of the opposition has said, this measure will not cure unemployment at the present time. Of course, it will not be of tremendous immediate value in regard to unemployment, and I doubt if it was designed for that purpose. However, in the long term view there is no question that it will be of benefit to our employment situation. It will have a tremendous effect on planning for the future of Canadians. This bill has been designed with a view to finding alternative uses for land which is submarginal or of low productivity in order to improve the economic role of those individuals on the land.
In my own constituency there are three great valleys, the Okanagan, the Kettle and the Similkameen. The Kettle valley is referred to as the sunshine valley in the Grand Forks area. One often wonders how far the government should go in respect of a project of this nature, and how much the progress should depend upon self-help. I have always advocated the principle that the government should not interfere too much, and I hope that this proposed act will be interpreted in that fashion. I hope the results of this measure will develop through co-operation between the governments and farm organizations. I would suggest that the farmers' problems should be forwarded to the government organizations for complete consideration before any drastic action is taken. This is my understanding of how it will be carried out.
In my area there has existed a great amount of what I term self-help. We have tackled our problem with hammer and tongs. We originally had a large ranching area but as a result of irrigation the area has developed to the point that it is now referred to as the


garden of Eden. We have had many problems which have been resolved through our own efforts. I was pleased that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) mentioned that which constitutes marginal land, and explained why this land which was previously good land has now lost its value. In our area there have been many causes in this respect, particularly regarding the fruit industry. One change has come about because of the change in consumer tastes. This change necessitated a change in the industry. This in itself presents a problem because in the fruit growing business one does not plant and harvest annually. As an example of this, let me point out that apple trees are planted and following a period of some ten years the fruit is harvested. The period of time involved in this process in respect of soft fruit is perhaps less, but this is the type of situation individuals in a fruit growing area must overcome.
In the Okanagan valley an attempt had been made to grow tobacco. In Oxford county there existed submarginal land and, it was wondered how the farmers would survive. Tobacco growing was introduced and it is significant that in that area today, since tobacco has become a crop, the farmers have taken tremendous strides forward. I understand the value of the tobacco crop in this area will run as high as $115 million this year. A tremendous portion of this money will return to the farmers. I cite this as an example of new usage of land.
Many things other than the change in consumer tastes have forced changes, such as the increase in competition for existing markets. This increase in competition has had a great effect upon the vegetable and fruit growing markets of the Okanagan. Shippers in the Okanagan are also faced with very high freight rates as a result of the distance to their markets. As a result of this distance the quality of our fruit has had to be improved, as of course it has, in order that the growers could survive in present day competitions for these markets in Canada.
Much of the land has been changed in regard to use in the Okanagan valley which, because of its climate and location, lends itself to the tourist industry. Some of the better growing land there has now been used for the establishment of motor courts. For my part I regret seeing this land turned into motor court areas. I have always felt that submarginal land should be used for this purpose rather than the fertile fruit growing land.
I would like to mention two other crops developed in my area. The first is the grape crop which, in the Okanagan valley and elsewhere in that area, is coming into being.

Wineries are being developed and are progressing successfully, and there are additional plans in existence to further this operation. I hope this experiment will be successful because there has been a lot of time and money invested.
The other crop I wish to mention is the tomato crop. There has been a decline in the growing of tomatoes in my area, and again there are many reasons for this decline. I would suggest the first reason is the increase in competition. I might say that up until 1956 we enjoyed rather a good tariff. For some reason or other, in 1956 the tariff was removed from tomatoes and consequently since that time we have suffered heavily as a result of paste and all forms of tomato goods being imported into Canada. I am not asking that the tariff be restored but consideration should be given to this and if the industry asks for it I will go after it.
I might mention the dominion experimental farm at Summerland, since this has to do with conservation and better use of soil. The farm at Summerland has done more than its fair share, as far as my area is concerned. This is particularly true when one considers the recent development of a new strain of tomatoes that will meet competition. They stand up well, can well and give a higher yield per acre.
As far as fruit is concerned, the experimental farm has been a leader all down the line in the development of new and suitable varieties for the Okanagan. This is also true in connection with pest control. Here they have been a leader and the growers of fruit throughout the valley take off their hats to those people who make up the staff of the dominion experimental farm. They are a devoted crew. I know that the thanks of the whole of the Okanagan goes out to them.
I said I had several main points that I wanted to bring up apart from the generalities I have just mentioned. My main points today are more or less twofold. They arise out of clause 4 of the bill. I do not know how far one can go in discussing this but let me say that we may expect the development and conservation of water supplies for agricultural purposes, soil improvement and conservation. We have had the problem of water supply for many years. The Okanagan and other valleys, apart from ranching, were of little use for agriculture until the advent of the irrigation system. We have had many irrigation projects. It is worth noting that as time has gone on replacement has had to take place in quite a number of irrigation systems. This is an expensive item. Consequently, I should like to see the government help in one way or another under this conservation bill in the use of water for farm
Marginal Lands Development irrigation purposes. There is no question but that the land itself cannot stand the additional charges occasioned by the replacement of all the major pipe lines and the control systems which have to go with them. This puts far too great a charge on the land.
As to the second point, soil improvement and conservation, I am looking mainly al conservation here. We have three valleys, namely the Similkameen through which the Similkameen river flows, the Okanagan, through which the Okanagan system flows, and the Kettle valley, which has the Kettle river. On the Okanagan river the provincial government, in conjunction with the federal government, on a 50-50 basis, has developed the Okanagan by water steps and by a damming system, and they have now so confined the river that there is very little overflowing and very little danger of flooding. Consequently, they have made it much easier for the farmers and ranchers situated along the river to plan ahead. They have also reclaimed many acres which are going to provide another source of land usage in the Okanagan, although they have not yet been put on the market. Of course, this will have a great benefit so far as the valley is concerned.
My reason for mentioning the Okanagan is that it did not require this legislation to do this work. This was a logical development. Action was taken, and more is planned. The Okanagan river itself is a smooth flowing system. It rises in the Okanagan lakes and, compared with other rivers, there is very little drop before it passes from Canada at Osoyoos into the United States across the border. It forms part of the Columbia system. On the other hand, in so far as erosion and soil conservation are concerned, the two rivers about which I should like to say something are first the Similkameen and second the Kettle, although not necessarily in that order. To my mind these two rivers are worth watching. Compared with the Okanagan, these rivers have a high rate of flow. In the spring they flow out to such an extent that the river becomes a danger to the lands along the banks. Each year some of the arable farmland disappears. Some farmers along the river banks have suffered grievously. They have lost everything. In other words, the river will take a swing and create havoc. If at all possible, we should have some form of control, some form of diking, or a dam, which will keep the river in a better temper.
Representations have been made by the United States counterparts on the Columbia river development. They have asked that the Similkameen be controlled. They have their reasons for that. Of course, they would like to put in power dams south of the border. A dam on the river would flood a considerable

Marginal Lands Development area in this part of Canada. To provide an even flow it is suggested that further dams should be erected. Just what effect this would have in Canada I do not know. I do not want to see any of our land flooded. I feel any control would have to be done by a series of stages up the river.
This is a river in which the government ought to be interested, particularly the Department of Veterans Affairs. There is a Veterans' Land Act project at Cawston which has a pumping station situated on the bank of the Similkameen and each year when the water is high there is a good cause for fear. Without water, as hon. members know, we will lose our trees. There is no question about it, the rainfall is not sufficient there. We must have irrigation. Therefore, I say the farmers look upon the recurrence of flooding with a great deal of fear.
Just recently I received another letter from the Cawston board of trade asking that I look into this and see whether something could not be done. If and when this legislation is enacted I ask that an inspection and a report be made on the river.
These are just two phases of various aspects of power, irrigation and control of the river, and we welcome any assistance which will aid the farmer along the way.
The same thing applies to the Kettle river. The Kettle has a more even temperament, a more even flow, than the Similkameen, but still it has the habit of taking great bites out of the land, and to my mind this is something which should be controlled. I need only say that in these mountain valleys it is important if possible to preserve that which we have. Soil is one thing, and I feel that we should go all out if possible and in the general interest do everything that we can to preserve our arable land.
When this legislation is passed I would ask that a survey be made of the Kettle river and all of its facets. We should decide whether it is possible to go ahead with some form or measure of control on this river to the end that we shall provide a better deal for all the farmers in the valley itself.
I was rather glad to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Pascoe) refer to the question of co-operation between governments. I know that when he spoke that way he also meant farm government, in other words, all farm organizations. This is essential, of course, and it is stated quite clearly in the provisions of the bill that the federal government is not going to do it by itself but in conjunction with the provincial governments which, of course, is the way it should be done. As I mentioned in

the earlier part of my speech, it is absolutely essential that we do not get too much government control but that, bearing in mind conservation and control of land use, all these various departments should work together in what are considered the best interests of all so that as a result we will have better use of our lands.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty in the circumstances to
join previous speakers in expressing my great satisfaction to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) for Bill No. C-77 now under discussion. The purpose of this bill is to empower the government to implement, in co-operation with the provinces, a policy for the rehabilitation of lands that are marginal or of low productivity.
When I spoke for the first time in this house during the budget debate, on June 26, 1958, I felt it was of great importance to bring this problem to the government's attention. In fact, as reported on page 1665 of Hansard in volume II for the session of 1958 I said this:
There are In my constituency a few communities where farms are not favoured with a loamy and very productive soil. Although I am no expert in this field, I nevertheless wish to refer to some suggestions made to me by several owners of such farms, to the effect that a grant for the claying of their land would be of great help since it would contribute to increase productivity and help them derive a better income from this land.
And I went on to say:
There is in Portneuf a provincial forestry school where, each year, sons of farmers follow seasonal classes. I feel that it would be wise to encourage by grants the reforestation of some parts of the unproductive farms, as this would create a substantial asset for the coming generation.
May I also bring to the attention of the minister, in order to stress the importance of this legislation, extracts from a lecture delivered before the chamber of commerce and the
Kiwanis club of the constituency of Portneuf by Mr. Armand Fafard, forestry engineer with the forestry information bureau of the Quebec department of lands and forests. His duties are to visit the farms and farm wood-lots where farmers wish to practice reforestation and to give farmers valuable advice about reforestation schemes or a more economical operation of farm woodlots.
In these circumstances I want to commend Mr. Fafard for the wonderful job he has done in the constituency of Portneuf where quite a number of farm plots call for rehabilitation through reforestation.

According to statistics I obtained from Mr. Fafard, 309 farm owners have planted 1,270,925 seedlings since 1946. This month 114 farm owners of that constituency will be planting 315,000 seedlings.
I should like to add that a few communities in my riding have taken a special interest in this reforestation policy and to mention the most important of them. For example, in the parish of Notre-Dame-des-Anges, since 1946, 351,500 seedlings were planted on 108 plantations; in St. Basile, 177,355 seedlings were planted, on 115 plantations; in Pont Rouge, 165,100 seedlings, on 82 plantations; in St. Raymond, 103,050 seedlings on 48 plantations, and in St. Ubald, where I live, 109,975 seedlings on 72 plantations. May I add that most of the communities in my riding have taken advantage of this policy.
I would also like to quote a few of the statements made by Mr. Fafard in a speech delivered before the members of the Kiwanis club and of the chamber of commerce.
The function of that office-the one referred to- which could also be called a forestry publicity service, is to encourage all woodlot owners to operate their woodlots successfully, to make owners more aware of the importance of the forest in the national, regional and domestic economy, to make them love and respect trees, to convince them that the forest, like farming land, must be attended to and improved, so that its products may gain in volume and value; in a word, its function is to teach the woodlot farmer about forestry, to provide him with such technical assistance he may need in the development of his woodlot or maple bush, in his reforestration operations and also in marketing his wood products.
And further:
We believe that, in the near future, the area of private woodlots will be extended considerably, because large areas, formerly used for agriculture, are no longer considered profitable. On these pieces of land, the natural growth is rather good when there are seed-trees in close proximity. Elsewhere, reforestation is a must.
I could thus go on reading these extracts to prove how important it is to concern ourselves with this problem of the reforestation of our farms.

In the lumber industry, the payroll amounts to $449,575.
In addition, the coal industry also contributes to the economy of Portneuf county.
It is therefore very important that we take some interest in those industries, because we can expect increased production in this field. If we want the economy to remain buoyant and if we want those companies to be in a position to obtain their materials from their present suppliers, we have to take an interest in the development of those industries.
I am glad to have had an opportunity to participate in this debate and I trust the people of Portneuf constituency will derive benefits from this bill.
For the information of Quebec farmers, I want to point out that many of them may not be aware of the existence of a provincial act which provides protection for those who engage in reforestation against any increase in municipal taxes. Here are a few excerpts of a pamphlet dealing with section 164 of this act:
I.	Who can benefit from section 164?
A person who plants a few hundred or a few thousand trees on his woodlot to complement natural regeneration: or a person who reforests a fraction of an acre of cleared land runs little risk of having his assessment raised as a result of his reforestation activities. On the other hand, any person planning to reforest cleared land over an area of an acre or more should avail himself of section 164. Assessors may, in preparing an assessment roll, ignore the fact that a portion of the property to be assessed is now covered with seedlings; however, there is no guarantee that they will in 10, 15 or 25 years hence, fail to take into account the promising stand that has grown from those seedlings. It is therefore wise to look to the future.
II.	What is required to enjoy the benefits of section 164?
A land owner who decides to reforest a particular area of his property need only, to avail himself of section 164, send notice in writing, before starting the work, to the secretary-treasurer of the municipality wherein is located the cadastral lot on which he plans to carry out reforestation, to the effect that he plans to reforest so many acres on the said lot and wishes to avail himself of section 164 of the Forests and Lands Act.
It is therefore most important that those interested in reforestation be aware of the benefits available under the act.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. members for allowing me to make these few remarks, and I again thank the minister for introducing a bill which will certainly benefit the citizens of the constituency of Portneuf.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been an interesting and useful debate. Indeed, during this session no

more important legislation will be debated than this bill introduced by my distinguished constituent, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton). For eastern Ontario, sir, and for my own county of Carleton in particular, this bill will be of basic and long range significance. I believe it will exert a profound influence upon our whole agricultural future.
For many years, I have believed, and in many speeches I have said, that fundamental to any long range, rational approach to the relief of agricultural problems is the institution of a genuine national soil and water conservation program. Accordingly, sir, I welcome wholeheartedly this measure designed for the achievement of such a program.
Essential to the success of any such program is that it be a genuinely co-operative effort of government-federal, provincial and municipal-community organizations, groups and individuals. That co-operation this legislation, as I understand it, will seek to achieve.
Under this bill three types of projects are contemplated. First, there are projects for the alternative use of farm lands which are submarginal, marginal or of low productivity. This development of alternative uses may include the encouragement of farm woodlots, tree farming, county forests, and reversion into crown lands. By providing for more effective utilization of marginal farm lands these projects in the long range will provide new sources of income for people in the area and to the extent that they remove marginal lands from farm use will help to reduce farm surpluses.
In the December, 1960 news bulletin of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture I was interested to see quoted with approval an extract from a speech made as long ago as 1951 by one of the finest citizens eastern Ontario has ever produced. I refer to the late hon. member for Lanark, Dr. W. G. Blair, whose untimely death cut off his career at the threshold of its greatest opportunity. These were the words of Dr. Blair:
With the per unit margin of profit growing smaller with each passing month, soon none but the best farms will be able to provide a decent standard of living for a farm family. With the demand for lumber growing each year, and with our forest reserves being cut rapidly, now would appear to be the ideal time to urge upon the proper authorities the need for reforesting all marginal and submarginal land that is now under cultivation. This would assure wood products for generations to come, and should provide a natural coverage to control the water level and spring run-off.

Those words of Dr. Blair quoted with approval by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture were prophetic, demonstrating as they did Dr. Blair's vigorous support for conservation, reforestation and intelligent land use.
The second type of project under this particular legislation contemplates the development of new income and employment opportunities for rural areas. With very great interest I have read the evidence taken before the Senate committee on land use. That is a committee which has done a most excellent job. I refer to the evidence regarding the success in many parts of the United States of the rural rehabilitation program in attracting local industry, developing recreational facilities, extending technical training, and encouraging a genuine community effort of self-help. The emulation of that effort in eastern Ontario would be most helpful. What has been done in so many United States communities, we can do in eastern Ontario and elsewhere in Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, this legislation contemplates joint projects with the provinces for the development and conservation of our water and soil resources. The introduction by the government of the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was an act of great constructive statesmanship. Under it large sums of public money have been expended to the great advantage of our western farmers and to the advantage of all Canada. In the mari-times, the Maritime Marshland Reclamation Act has been showing excellent results. In many of the valleys of old Ontario simply superlative conservation work is being done. This legislation heralds the placing of these programs of soil and water conservation on a truly national basis.
However, I believe it would be unfortunate if the house were to treat these projects as isolated ones insulated from other aspects of agricultural policy. In fact, the projects now proposed are an integral part of the whole agricultural program related directly to the fundamental issue of price stabilization, the problem of disposal of farm surpluses, the extension of adequate farm credit facilities and the provision of crop insurance.
Mr. Speaker, the objective of agricultural policy must be to establish and retain family-owned, family-sized farm units, but units of such size and efficiency that will enable the farm family to earn an income equivalent to that earned by those in other comparable vocations with comparable investment.
90205-6-282J
Marginal Lands Development
During the past 15 years, agriculture has experienced a virtual revolution in technology, farm methods and techniques. Agricultural scientists today are in general agreement that mechanization and other technological advances have rendered obsolete the traditional 100-acre unit of eastern Ontario except for highly specialized production. As one observes the extent of abandonment of farm lands in eastern Ontario-or the partial abandonment with owners running a few stockers and grazers and gaining their principal income from "off-farm" employment-the opinion of the technical agriculturalists appears to be confirmed. Yet there are still many small farm units in my county of Carleton which, under intensive cultivation and efficient management, are producing for their owners satisfactory returns and which give indication of continuing to do so.
In any consideration of agricultural policy we must never lose sight of the fact that the family-owned, family-operated farm is a social institution. Such a farm has a threefold significance. It is a business venture; it is a home; it is a way of life. Let it never be forgotten that the integrity of the farm home has been a basic reason for the strength of our Canadian nationhood.
In that most valuable study of Canadian agriculture entitled "Progress and Prospects of Canadian Agriculture" prepared by Dr. W. M. Drummond and Mr. William Mackenzie for the royal commission on economic prospects, there is at page 316 a discussion of the net income per farm by provinces, the study of which I would commend to all hon. members. The table appearing at that page shows that the 1951-55 average net farm income was $2,772, a very meagre return indeed for the farm family upon the invested capital and labour involved. This figure varies from a low of $963 in Nova Scotia to a high of $3,758 in Saskatchewan.
I confess that I was somewhat taken aback by the table which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) placed on Hansard at page 1403 in presenting the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill. The table indicated that, according to the economic classification of farms in the 1956 census, 21 per cent of Canadian farms produced less than $1,200 worth of produce annually; that out of a total of 575,015 farms 120,242 produced less than $1,200. This is subsistence farming at its worst.
What unfortunately has happened in the older sections of Canada is that many farmers have made their living out of depreciation; depreciation of their soil resources, their buildings, their fences. Depreciation of their capital assets generally has provided the profit from which the farmers survived.

Marginal Lands Development
Many more farmers close to the urban areas above become increasingly dependent upon off-farm employment and earnings. On such a basis a healthy farm industry cannot be founded.
As a nation Canada has been the most profligate of all countries in her treatment of her greatest natural asset, the upper six inches of our soil. The depredations made upon those upper six inches is little short of appalling. We now see where that profligacy is leading us. We now recognize that we cannot afford longer to be so profligate with this greatest of all our natural assets, and this legislation constitutes an intelligent and courageous advance in meeting the problem of soil and water conservation.
Throughout Canada the last 15 years have brought about a major reorganization of farm businesses, including a reduction in the number of farms and an enlargement of the average size of farm. This process of consolidation has meant an increase in the need for capital for additional machines and larger inventories of producing livestock.
Technological processes have increased production per acre and per animal. The adjustment of agricultural production to the use of mechanical power and the application of new techniques of production has taken place with really astonishing rapidity, and has not only increased the volume of production per acre and per animal but has brought about a reduction in the labour force to only 70 per cent of the pre-war level.
A statistical analysis of farming in my own county of Carleton is both interesting and relevant. In 1951 there were 3,104 farms in the county of Carleton having a total acreage of 473,644 acres. By 1956, the latest date for which census statistics are available, the number of farms had declined to 2,743 with a total acreage of 444,509 acres. So in just five years 361 families had left the farm and 29,135 acres had been taken out of agricultural production. That trend has unfortunately continued at an accelerated pace.
In 1951 the average area per farm in Carleton county was 152.6 acres. By 1956 consolidation of holdings had raised the average acreage to 162.1 acres.
The statistics of the sizes of Carleton county farms are interesting. Of the 2,743 farms in 1956 there were 800 farms of less than 70 acres; these would be mostly market gardens supplying the city of Ottawa. There were 1,120 farms of between 70 and 130 acres; 679 farms of between 130 and 240 acres; 116 farms of between 240 acres and 400 acres; 24 farms of between 400 and 760 acres, and four farms of over 760 acres.

Mr. Speaker, the government of Ontario has recently published a most excellent booklet called "An economic survey of the eastern Ontario region", that region which we who live in it know colloquially as the golden triangle. To all hon. members I commend the reading of this interesting publication from which I have drawn my statistics, covering as it does the area from Kingston on the St. Lawrence through to the Quebec boundary and up the Ottawa river from the riding of my hon. friend from Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Villeneuve) to the most northerly section of the riding of Renfrew North.
For eastern Ontario there is another aspect of this legislation to which I should draw attention. I believe this proposed legislation should have an especially profound effect in the national capital region. One of the objectives of the national capital plan has been to provide a balanced urban-rural development in this area on both sides of the Ottawa river. The acquiring of the Gatineau park on the Quebec shore and the institution of a green belt on the Ontario side are basically designed for that purpose.
Within the green belt it is essential that proper conservation techniques should be employed; measures of the type envisaged by this legislation, reforestation of the submarginal lands, control of erosion, control of water resources, scientific development and utilization of the productive lands. This is essential, and it is essential now, unless the green belt is to become a weed belt, which the people of Canada would never tolerate.
Outside the green belt, in Carleton and in the constituency of my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Tardif), the provisions of this legislation have special significance. A balanced rural development, with new population concentrated into properly planned hamlets, is essential to the nation's capital.
The gradual taking out of production of marginal and submarginal lands, their reforestation, the control of the rivers and creeks, the control of spring run-off and conservation of our water resources, the prevention of pollution-these essential features can be achieved under this legislation with the co-operation of the provinces and the municipalities.
The more productive lands will be freed from the depressing effects of surpluses; they will have greater stability of income, greater opportunity for capital improvement of soil resources through drainage and improved cultivation, for improvement of farm buildings and fences.
In this generally rich agricultural area of eastern Ontario I can foresee this legislation meaning a general "face-lift" so that Ottawa,

which is the shire town, the county town of Carleton, as well as being the nation's capital, will be surrounded by a balanced, profitable agricultural development.
Mr. Speaker, the true need of agriculture is not some gaudy panacea; it is not some cure-all. It is the establishment of positive objectives for agriculture, the acceptance of equity for agricultural producers as a fundamental right and the recognition that this must be achieved by progressive steps, deliberately taken, based upon sensible, rational, social and economic principles.
As I searched for a way to express to the house my deep conviction on this subject there came to my mind a speech made 18 years ago by a great Canadian, a leader of my party, a man whose dedication to the cause of agriculture has been the abiding crusade, the overwhelming ambition, of his life. These are the words of John Bracken spoken to the Holstein-Friesian breeders' association on February 3, 1943:
It is not foreordained that farmers as a class shall work for less pay than anybody else;
or have their children receive, in many areas, only one quarter of the chance of a secondary education or one tenth of the chance of a university education that other children get;
or see their wives forced by economic circumstances into lives of toil, often 12 but sometimes 14 hours a day, all too often Sundays and holidays included.
Fortunately, these statistics have improved in the past 18 years, particularly since 1957. I continue:
These things are not inevitable, and they are not creditable to Canada.
There is no just reason why any farm people in Canada should be forced into the position of poor relations of the rest of society.
No one in urban life that I know of wants to see an inferior economic status fastened upon rural people. No one deliberately plans to keep rural people at these disadvantages.
Farmers don't want handouts from the state. They want markets at fair prices for what they produce. Failing that, they want-and have every justification for expecting-a fair relationship to exist between the prices of what they sell and the prices of what they buy and have to pay for, including labour. They want a square deal. They ask for no more than that; and society cannot, in decency, give them less.
Sir, these words of this outstanding Canadian come ringing back to me 18 years later, for they express more adequately than any words of my own could, my attitude toward agricultural policy. They express the basic objective of this government.

This government is erecting an edifice of balanced, co-ordinated farm policy designed to cure the situations described by Mr. Bracken. It has four cornerstones; each cornerstone is a legislative advance achieved since 1957. Basic is price stabilization, provided by the agricultural products stabilization act, designed to prevent violent fluctuations in price. On the second corner is the Farm Credit Act, a major advance from the old farm loan board; and on the third, the Crop Insurance Act; and now with this agricultural rehabilitation and development bill the fourth cornerstone is laid and the edifice of a balanced agricultural policy may be proceeded with.
Mr. Speaker, it was fluid milk at 80 cents a hundred which drove me from the farm and which educated me in the law. The memories of farm prices at those disaster levels made me resolve that if ever it was my privilege to serve my fellow citizens, my first dedication would be to an attempt to bring to the farmers of my native historic Carleton a position of social and economic equality with those in other callings. I proclaim that as the first principle of my political creed, and because this bill is a major step toward the achievement of that aim-that principle-it has my enthusiastic support.

While in the city of Charlottetown not long ago I had the opportunity of attending a Rotary club luncheon in honour

Marginal Lands Development of the Prince Edward Island winners of outstanding prizes at the royal winter fair, and it was stated there that never in the history of a province had there been so many winners.
Following the example of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill)-and I follow his example in so many things-I am emboldened to speak in regard to this agricultural field. Similarly, as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), whose eloquence and experience far surpasses mine, I have been especially moved by this bill because it is one of those fundamental pieces of legislation which deals not merely with an institution or an ad hoc situation, but with something very vital and fundamental not only to our way of life but indeed to life itself. I can remember as a small boy hearing the member of parliament for Queens county, the late Mr. Myers, make a speech, and I have never forgotten his words. He said the whole of life, and all that life has become, depends entirely upon the top six inches of the soil covering the earth. Surely the farmer and the agriculturist must be the first citizen of us all in terms of importance. Surely it is an ancient and honourable industry.
A writer who has always impressed me by the depth of his thought and the width of his vision was Louis Bromfield, who was always so concerned with the way we North Americans denuded the great resources which were found on this continent, and how we mined the soil so often instead of working it properly, and how the riches, which were here when the settlers from Europe came, have so often been diminished and indeed denuded.
No one from my province, so far as I know, has participated in this debate but, because Prince Edward Island is called the million acre farm, and I think quite rightly, I am happy to say that this bill will be most meaningful and helpful to that province which is known as the garden province. When the hon. minister and his expert officials continue their study of the resources involved in this vast frontal attack which they have embarked upon, they will find that much of the work has already been done in Prince Edward Island. As is stated in the dust jacket of the book, he went back to a time before the potato was born. That is a fairly long time. The book includes tremendously accurate and

comprehensive sets of statistics which I would commend to the experts of the minister's department who will be carrying on statistical studies in relation to this legislation.
Prince Edward Island, like the area mentioned by the hon. member who has just spoken, has long been a region of small farms and independent farmers. We have always had limited acreage, and if it were not for the fact that we were able to produce excellent crops such as the potato-the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) is not in the house so perhaps I will affirm that the Prince Edward Island potato is the outstanding potato of any on the market-we might have suffered from some of those things the hon. member has just mentioned.
We have not suffered from a decline in farm income as the recent statistics indicate, but there has been a steady departure from farms. Although the province of Prince Edward Island, in recent years has had an increase in population, it is not as populous now as it was in the 1890's. The 1891 census showed a population of 105,000 people. It is only recently that we have again reached the 100,000 mark. This arises from the departure from the farms of many of our young people. My colleague the Minister of Fisheries once said that the polling district in which he lives has now as many people on the voter's list as were qualified to vote in the days before the women of the country were given the franchise. The number of our abandoned and vacant farms is, I think, the most fundamental problem in our province. It is fundamental not only in agricultural terms but in human terms, because it indicates the constant export of our greatest resource, our young people, to other parts of the continent. For a long time, as everyone knows, the maritime provinces contributed to the great intellectual development of New England and there are very few maritime families that do not have a branch or two in New England, that intellectual heart of the republic. In the maritimes we are now contributing to the growth of Toronto. Probably this is one of the reasons why this city is developing so rapidly and reaching a degree of acceptance that it did not have in years gone by.
The future of agriculture in Prince Edward Island will be brightened by what this bill foretells. We must have not so much more specialization but greater diversification. Vacant farms must be brought into productivity. A wider range of agricultural commodities must be developed. Within the last two or three years we have been developing with great success tobacco crops in the eastern portion of our province. This offers new vistas. This is also true of activities in

the small fruits field, and certainly in reforestation. In the early days, as Professor Clark points out, there were great stands of pine in Prince Edward Island. It was a heavily forested province. It has not been denuded of trees nor has it suffered from unwise cutting down of forests which has caused erosion in so many parts of Canada, but nevertheless there are areas which might now be turned to profitable forest production.
I may say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) that, when he starts his activity, which is a co-operative venture, he will find few provinces better prepared in a legislative way than the province of Prince Edward Island. In that province we already have an exhaustive plan for a comprehensive resources survey, an economic development program which will dovetail magnificently with this A.R.D.A. bill.
I should like to particularize; I should like to be specific, as was the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), but at this stage I will say only generally that in the A.R.D.A. bill we have but one more of those pieces of legislation which will do a great deal to bring not only material gain to the maritime provinces but an uplift in spirit, because agriculture in the maritime provinces needs this. For instance we are today importing things which we should be exporting. Leadership, mobilization of ability from the dominion authority, co-operation with the provincial governments, will fit in with the new spirit that prevails in our eastern seaboard provinces and will bring to our major and ancient industry a new feeling of confidence which we hope will be reflected in an increase in population, in an increased diversity to our income. It is another forward step, and there have been a great many in the last four years, to bridge that gap which too long has existed in economic standards between the maritime provinces and the rest of Canada.
Because I firmly believe that this is one of the most imaginative steps that has been taken by the government, I heartily endorse this A.R.D.A. bill and commend the minister on his vision and initiative in bringing it forward.

Believe me, sir, I live in the province of Alberta and I remember when the government under the leadership of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was formed. He introduced the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. It was his own initiative; it was established by him and his government, and it has continued to this day.
With regard to the comment made by my friend from Bonavista-Twillingate, let me say that Mr. Gardiner made a very fine political vehicle out of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act for a good many years. In the west we are concerned with this bill. We think it is long overdue. We would have liked to see

Marginal Lands Development it many years ago. We now have it. It means a great deal to us. There are large areas in western Canada-and I think no one realizes this more than the Minister of Agriculture- which, by reason of deficient rainfall and certain other natural impoverishments, simply cannot continue on a crop production basis.
My hon. friend from Queens talked about trees; my hon. friend from Carleton talked about market gardening in the Ottawa area. They have their problems. Our problem is that of tremendous tracts of land without too sound a basis. Our objective must be changed. We must bring about some reforms. We must convert large areas now devoted to the plow, the seed drill and the binder or reaper, to natural grass as was the case many years ago.
I have said in the house before that a large section of western Canada lies within what we call the Palliser triangle, an area of very limited rainfall. Last week I was in my constituency on official business and what did I find? I found that we have had no rainfall and very little snowfall. Each year for the last four years we have had less and less precipitation, and I hope the minister will appreciate in relation to the bill before us, that each year for the last four years we have moved more and more toward the drought conditions of the thirties.
As far as I am concerned as a resident of western Canada, as one who has spent his adult life in Alberta, I feel that a very grave emergency is arising. I am delighted that finally, for the first time in the history of Canada, we are to have a comprehensive program which seeks to alleviate and control the problem we face in the prairie provinces.
I have spoken before of the diminishing water supply in western Canada. We are building the South Saskatchewan dam and I think one of the reasons it is being rushed to completion is the small supply of domestic water in the towns and villages of Saskatchewan. This reduced supply of domestic water comes about by virtue of the fact that each year the run-off from the eastern shed of the Rockies is less and less. That is true of my district. I live in an area which has 200,000 irrigated acres and we have witnessed with alarm the receding water supply. We need water conservation and this bill promises it to us. I should like to commend the minister and to say to him and through him to the government which I am proud to support, that this is one of the most progressive steps, agriculturally, that has been taken by any government in the history of Canada.
