This program will be of great assistance to the farm families. The government has always taken a great interest in farm families. A farm family is rather hard to define but I would say it is the family that believes that farming is a way of life and a wonderful education for young people. Some of our great men were farm boys and benefited from the education they received.
This bill refers to the development of alternative economic uses for marginal agricultural land. Examples of this are the encouragement of farm woodlots, of tree farming, of county forests, of reversion into crown lands, recreational areas and so on in eastern Canada. Last year, Mr. Speaker, I was fortunate enough to be able to travel through eastern Canada. I saw these small farms at that time which consisted of a few acres under cultivation and on which there was a milk cow. The farmer was trying to raise a family on the income derived from these farms. I noticed the same situation in parts of Quebec and New Brunswick. I feel that this bill will be of great assistance to these farmers because they will be able to start in the wood business and in the production of pulpwood. I admit that it will take years to see any results from this program. At least it is a start toward assisting these farmers to earn a livelihood for their families.
The conversion to grass of marginal cropping land in western Canada by means of 90205-6-283
Marginal Lands Development the community pasture technique and encouraging wildlife habitat areas, recreation development and crop diversification are other examples. In certain parts of the west there is land being farmed which should be turned over to grass for the production of cattle. This step could be taken under this act with the assistance of the government. Some of this land has been farmed for years, and this year, particularly in my part of Alberta, we have noticed that the water level has dropped drastically. Many people who have cattle are already concerned about water and pasture. If we do not get our June rains, some of these people are going to be in dire circumstances. It is comforting to realize that under this act a program for water conservation could be developed.
Just recently the P.F.R.A. organization has moved into our area. The farmers are now able to obtain dams and dugouts, so there is going to be an abundance of water for the cattle. This government changed the farm loan board to the farm credit corporation, and this move is working out very well. The young farmer is able to get a start through the credit provided by this organization, and those farmers already established can expand their operations into an economic unit.
These community pastures are very important. There are a few of them being organized in Alberta. I am very interested in a tract of land in my constituency which was purchased by the previous government to add to the Wainwright army camp. This land is used for army manoeuvres for only two or three weeks during the year. I would be interested in having the Department of Agriculture investigate the possibility of making better use of that land by turning it into a community pasture. Many of our farmers are short of pasture land and, therefore, have had to reduce the size of their herds. They are going to find it very difficult to finance their operations if they cannot keep cattle on their farms.
I do not think I should take up much more of the time of the house, but I should like to express my thanks to the minister for all the work he has done in connection with this measure.

One of these, of course, is that we have eliminated all the reserves for water conservation in the agricultural areas and we are now experiencing a terrific run-off of our topsoil in many parts of this area. Thank you Mr. Speaker. I was therefore saying that, as a member from the province of Quebec, it give me great pleasure to support the motion of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) for second reading of Bill C-77.
In describing myself as a member from the province of Quebec, I do not intend to infer that I do not regard myself as a member for the other provinces of Canada. However, our Liberal opponents often make it a point to accuse the members from Quebec of not supporting the principle of certain bills coming under the joint jurisdiction of the federal and provincial governments. I know this to be a fact because I have read about it in a number of newspapers and have often heard
Marginal Lands Development it stated in this house. In certain remarks which were intended to be either amusing or critical, some Liberal members from Quebec and Newfoundland have suggested that the members from the province of Quebec always drag their feet when it comes to such measures, or even ignore them completely.
Mr. Speaker, when, in the past and in recent times, the members from the province of Quebec or the government of the province have opposed certain bills introduced by the federal government, it was because they had to in view of certain conditions and in the interest of their province.
The Liberals have, in the past, taken us to task for failing to take a stand on some of those bills.
It gives me pleasure to say that in this case, the members from the province of Quebec as a group support this piece of legislation.
First of all, the bill deals with something which, under the constitution, comes under the joint responsibility of the provinces and the federal government.
Of course, it concerns the disposal of part of the provincial territories, but it must be noted that this measure respects the provisions of the constitution regarding the ownership of the lands, the soil and the territory, since the federal government will not undertake any step unless there has been a previous agreement with the province concerned.
This is an example of the kind of bill introduced by a Conservative government which is respectful of the rights of the provinces, and is at the same time anxious to fulfill its duties towards the people of Canada. This is a relief after the centralizing bills of the previous era when Liberals always used to introduce measures designed to make gradual inroads upon provincial jurisdiction in certain fields, so that they might take advantage of those infringements to increase their responsibility, and then refuse to leave the taxation fields they had grabbed during the war.
The Conservative attitude is quite different. We do not deny the existence of national problems. The problem of the distribution of arable land is one of them.
Here you have this Conservative government, respecting the constitution and the jurisdiction of the provinces, introducing a bill that takes into account the constitutional framework, which must always be taken into consideration when it is a matter of legislating for the whole of Canada.
Therefore, I want to congratulate not only the Minister of Agriculture, but the whole cabinet, for their initiative in introducing this bill entitled:

Marginal Lands Development
Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act.
Mr. Speaker, if I were allowed to make a few remarks about the implementation of this bill, I would ask the government to see to it that, when regulations are adopted in relation to this bill, they, as well as the agreements signed between the various provinces, should be flexible enough to apply to the particular problems of each province.
There is not one province where farm problems or rural establishment problems are not altogether different from those in other provinces.
In the province of Quebec, agriculture is mostly based on the family farm principle and this will create a problem, namely the avoidance of anything that would tear whole families away from their usual surroundings for the purpose of establishing them elsewhere. Certain difficulties would arise then. But I am sure that, with the wholehearted co-operation of every provincial government, the problems will be easily settled between the parties involved, through the agreements provided in this bill.
I shall not venture to discuss the problems of other provinces, because I know that my colleagues from other provinces, especially Conservative members, are qualified to do so. However, I shall endeavour to point out in particular the problems facing the government in a possible agreement with the government of the province of Quebec.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I take the liberty of requesting of the premier of the province of Quebec that he refrain from playing petty politics in this field, as he appeared to indicate during the last federal-provincial conferences on fiscal matters. I know that the premier of Quebec has only recently become a convert to autonomy but he does not seem to understand it thoroughly-

Twenty five years of progress.
While we here in south Alberta are showing special interest in the resources for tomorrow conference scheduled for the coming autumn, it seems worth while to recall that just a quarter century ago one of the finest pieces of legislation in the history of the west was passed by parliament at Ottawa.
That was the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, for which we give full credit to the late hon. Robert Weir, then minister of agriculture in the Bennett government, and a farmer of the Melfort, Saskatchewan, constituency, who brought the measure into the house at a time when the prairie west was in a parlous state due to a combination of the lowest world price for wheat in 400 years, plus drought, plus soil drifting with its black blizzards.
Our problem in the Fraser valley is not like that of a good many other places where water is in short supply. We very often have too much water and the problem is one of drainage. All hon. members will recall the floods of 1948 and 1950. Dikes were built and after they were completed in 1949 and 1950 the understanding was that the provincial government would assume the responsibility of keeping them in good condition.
During the last winter quite a number of authorities in the Fraser valley have come to the view that the dikes have greatly deteriorated. Not only have they become lower but water gets in under them and erodes the foundation and some of the dikes are falling into the river. The board of trade of Mission City has organized quite an effort to try to get the federal government to assist in putting the dikes back into shape and they are supported by several boards of trade in the Fraser valley, those of Chilliwack, Abbotsford, Hope, Langley and so on, and also by the associated boards of trade. There is great fear that if a flood does occur some spring the result will be disastrous. If such a flood should take the same form as on the last occasion the cost would be a very serious matter not

I should like to refer to the pamphlet explaining the bill and to correct a misapprehension as to the farming situation in British Columbia. It is indicated in the pamphlet that 46 per cent of the farms in that province have an annual income of less than $1,200. It is also shown that the figures for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are higher. I suggest that the reason for this is that we have a lot of part-time farmers in British Columbia, people who have small acreages and who may also be fishermen or lumbermen. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to bring about a greater measure of conservation, improved land use and an improvement in agricultural income by means of various projects. We were pleased to support the resolution which preceded the bill and we shall vote for second reading of the bill. However, the fact that the government has introduced a measure of this kind does not tell us to what extent the government hopes to use the measure or to what extent the provinces are prepared to co-operate with the federal government. It tells us absolutely nothing about the amount of money or even the proportion of money that the government will provide for these various projects.


In introducing the resolution the minister told us he wanted to place the bill on the order paper, have first reading and then he would go back and forth across the country meeting the farm organizations and provincial governments in order to discuss projects under this bill and to learn the attitude of the provinces and the farm organizations so that he would be in a position to change the bill in any way that seemed advisable. I hope that when he closes the debate he will inform us as to how many provincial governments he has interviewed, how many are interested in this measure, how many projects he thinks may be forthcoming under the measure during the present year and to what extent the federal government is prepared to put money into this measure. After all, it is not going to be good enough to have on the record a well-worded long term program unless the government is prepared to push it.
It is fine for hon. members on the other side to get up and compliment the minister and express great support for and faith in the measure, but we are not quite so confident that the government is going to use the measure to the fullest possible extent. We have had other rather bitter experiences in the house of the government introducing measures that read well, were promoted most capably and were given a tremendous amount of publicity but under which the farmers have found they got less than under the legislation replaced by these measures and the programs for which the new legislation was substituted. I refer, of course, to the old bill 237 under which the government has allowed the prices of eggs and hogs to collapse. Therefore it is necessary to have more than good phraseology, well meaning statements and complimentary remarks.
This has been a Conservative field day, almost a Conservative filibuster, although it does not bother me too much if the Conservatives want to put forward a dozen or more speakers on the same day one after the other. The main theme of these speakers has been that the minister is a great fellow, that this is a wonderful bill, that they are a fine party, that the Liberals were in power for 22 years and did nothing and that the people had to wait for a Conservative government to introduce a measure of this kind aimed at the conservation of agricultural resources.
This bill has a title. We know that the government is stuck with the title of the act before the bill has been approved by the house. They have used the title on a pamphlet. I think it was rather insulting to parliament that the government should bring out a pamphlet entitled, "Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act" before parliament had approved or the governor general had

given royal assent to that act. I think this is an affront to the House of Commons. This is a rather stupid way to conduct public business. speechtext:
The hon. member not only wants to tell me what I am saying but where to look when I am saying it.
Under the community pastures project under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act-and it is a very important development-a great deal has been done. A tremendous number of acres have been brought under the community pastures system. Land has been regrassed. There has been allocated and reserved for grass land which might otherwise have been put under the plow when it was not suitable for that purpose. The total area of land in pastures as shown at the end of this report for 1958-59 was 1,815,265 acres. Yet if one looks back at the acreage given under this project, one finds none before 1938. In other words prior to 1938 under a Conservative government not a single community pasture had been established. There are 64 community pastures today. The records show that 61 were established under the former Liberal government and that three have been established during this government's period in office.
I therefore suggest that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has proved to be a good act under which many worth-while projects have been established. I suggest that it is not accurate to say that under a Liberal administration nothing was done in this field. The fact of the matter is that members in all parts of the house, in all parties, over the years have been very much interested in conservation. John R. MacNicol, a long time Conservative member of the House of Commons, used to make this matter almost a full-time cause. Although he had little connection with the prairie areas or the agricultural areas of Canada, representing as I believe he did, a constituency in the city of Toronto, nevertheless, I think even the members of the Liberal party and the house will agree that he made an important contribution to conservation and to agricultural development.
Marginal Lands Development

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner was prepared to give him credit for that contribution. Therefore, I do not think it should be necessary for the members on the government side of the house to try to pretend that nothing was done until this government arrived on the scene and that all of a sudden, by bringing in this bill and by printing a pamphlet and distributing it, agricultural conservation or improvement of soil productivity has become the order of the day.
When I rose, Mr. Speaker, I said that what we are really going to be interested in is to learn from the Minister of Agriculture the projects he has under way with the provinces or how many projects will be established. We wish to learn from him whether any provincial government intends to establish any projects during the present year and whether this program really will be under way and in operation during the current year. I should like to know the proportion of these projects that the federal government is prepared to finance.
I say to the government now that they had better do better under this act than they have done under the Crop Insurance Act. Twenty per cent will not do the job. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act the federal government paid the whole shot. The provincial governments and the community pastures provided much of the land. As far as dug-outs are concerned, the farmers have put up some money. It has been a smaller amount in recent years because the proportion paid by the federal government has been increased. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act, another act in the field of the maintenance of farm income about which this act has some things to say, has been paid for by the federal government and by the farmers, and under that act there was no endeavour to load the financial responsibility on the provinces.
I am not saying that the provinces have not some responsibility. I think they have some responsibility. I am not saying that the provinces should not be asked to contribute something under this act. However, I express the hope that, more in keeping with the responsibility accepted by the federal government under P.F.R.A. and under P.F.A.A., the federal government will accept the major financial responsibility and will not endeavour to foist it on either the provincial governments or the agricultural producers themselves. This act could be an excellent one. Time will tell. The administration of the measure will determine its real value, but I can tell hon. gentlemen opposite that in my

Marginal Lands Development judgment the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has been a good one and much has been accomplished through that act. This will need to be a very good act before it justifies replacing the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
I think the two can work together, and before we junk one we should be certain that this bill adds a great deal to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and does in fact bring about a very important extension of that act.

I recall very distinctly the speeches-I must say they were sometimes a little repetitious in the sense that they were repeated year after year; but I only say that by way of commendation of the hon. member-of the late hon. member, Mr. MacNicol.
